posts.text: Vickman @stratton001 Introducing STYX — built at NEAR HACKATHON on @NEARProtocol to bring scoped spending, delivery verification, and owner-controlled payments to agent services. As agents take on more useful work, one question becomes harder to ignore: how do we let them coordinate services without giving them unrestricted control over our money? An agent completing a task and a service requesting payment are only parts of the process. Someone still needs to define the rules, check what was delivered, and decide whether that delivery deserves payment. That is the workflow we built with STYX. HOW IT WORKS The current use case is turning structured invoices into accounting CSV files. An owner prepares a job and defines its scope, spending cap, permitted service, recipient, expiry, and delivery requirements. STYX compares service quotes and connects the selected work to those rules. The delivery then goes through deterministic checks for source coverage, arithmetic, duplicates, uncertainty, and integrity. The owner can inspect the actual CSV and verification results before accepting the work. For the NEAR testnet flow, the owner reviews and signs the relevant wallet actions. Buyer-agent, provider, and verifier roles use separate identities; they do not receive the owner’s wallet keys. A verified result can proceed to owner-approved payment. Failed checks block acceptance, and a reservation can be released without paying the provider. WHAT WE HAVE WORKING • Structured JSON/CSV invoice processing. • Local parsing, with optional NEAR AI extraction behind explicit data-sharing and API-cost consent. • Owner-defined rules and spending caps. • Service quote comparison. • Downloadable CSV deliveries and source comparisons. • Separate buyer-agent, provider, verifier, and owner roles. • NEAR testnet escrow, reservation, delivery, verification, and payment flows. • Transaction reconciliation that checks final receipts and contract state after interrupted or uncertain submissions. • Completed testnet payment and reservation-release examples. WHY BUILD THIS ON NEAR? STYX uses NEAR testnet to record and enforce the agreement and settlement flow, while keeping invoice contents off-chain. The application connects the work people can inspect with the payment actions owners authorize. A wallet redirect alone is not treated as settlement: STYX reconciles the transaction and contract state before reporting confirmation. The broader idea is a reusable pattern for agent services: bounded authority, inspectable delivery evidence, and explicit owner control over payment. TRY IT WITHOUT A WALLET We also built a public sample workspace so anyone can explore the product immediately. You can load 30 fictional invoices, set a spending cap, compare quotes, inspect the generated CSV, accept a successful delivery, or try an arithmetic-failure case and release the reservation. Each visitor gets an isolated temporary workspace. Sample payments are clearly labelled simulations and do not send NEAR. Separate proof links show earlier, actual NEAR testnet transactions. WHERE WE ARE TODAY STYX is a working testnet pilot. Both configured service providers are currently STYX-operated, and the verifier runs on a trusted server. The checks establish consistency with the supplied invoice data; they do not prove invoice authenticity. Independent security review, broader user testing, and operational hardening remain ahead before commercial use. We would love feedback from NEAR builders, agent developers, and people who work with invoice processing: what evidence would you need before allowing an agent-assisted workflow to release payment? But giving an agent direct access to a wallet and its assets comes with serious risks. @Arashb122 and I worked on this exact problem with PrivatePay Agent. How can you allow an agent to make payments without giving it direct and unlimited control over assets??? In PrivatePay Agent, sensitive invoice information is first redacted locally. If any restriction is violated, the payment is blocked and the failed attempt is recorded onchain. If it fails, the provider can retry. If time runs out, the escrow is refunded to the owner Any independent AI agent can use it. Right now you mostly get two options.

Give the agent the keys, and one bad prompt or one bug can empty the wallet.

Or approve every payment yourself, and then it's not really an autonomous agent anymore.

Neither one scales.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
BILA sits in the middle.

You fund a treasury. You set the rules. The agent can only ask to spend from it.

A smart contract on NEAR checks every request and either approves it or blocks it.

The AI model never holds the money.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
What happens when a request comes in:

Inside the limits: approved, reserved, settled on chain.
Above the per-payment cap: blocked.
Small, but today's budget is already used: blocked.

The agent gets a plain reason back every time.

posts.author: xbtonchaine
posts.text:
Why the agent can't cheat:

Its key can only call one function, request_payment.
It can't attach money or change its own limits.
Raising a limit needs your wallet signature.
You can pause or revoke an agent any time, no deposit needed.

That's BILA. Live on Near.

Making a market is expensive. Someone has to quote prices 24/7, commit capital, manage inventory and absorb risk.

For the long tail, the economics rarely make sense.

So I started with a question:

What if the market maker was just a formula?

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
That's ZeroTick.

You bring a signed reference price with your trade.

The contract verifies it, computes an executable quote, and settles against a shared USDC vault.

No constantly posted on-chain quotes. No tokenized underlying. No dedicated liquidity pool per asset.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
Here's where it gets interesting.

The formula prices risk dynamically.

Stale data? Wider spreads.
Higher volatility? More expensive quotes.
Pool getting crowded? Prices adjust.
Risk limits hit? Trade rejected.
The pricing curve continuously adapts to protect liquidity.

posts.author: blasrodri
posts.text:
And every position has its maximum payout capped and reserved upfront.

The vault won't accept a trade it can't collateralize.

One pool can back many markets, with separate risk limits.

LPs don't need to seed every pair or actively post quotes.

That's the real innovation.

OTC Markets handled ~$691B in 2025.
